title: Southeast Asia's Oldest Sanskrit Stone
place: Võ Cạnh village, near Nha Trang, Khánh Hòa, Vietnam
text: A four-sided sandstone pillar from Võ Cạnh carries Brahmi-script lines, partly in Sanskrit verse, praising a king of the Sri Mara family, founder of Champa's first dynasty. Phrases about compassion for all beings show Buddhist influence from India. Vietnam's National Museum of History calls it the earliest evidence of Sanskrit reaching Champa, and the oldest stone in Southeast Asia to show India's influence.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Vo Canh stele

title: The Many Faces of Maitum
place: Ayub Cave, Pinol, Maitum, Sarangani, Mindanao, Philippines
text: In a Mindanao cave, people reburied selected bones in clay jars whose lids were shaped as human heads, each with its own expression: male or female, young or old, happy or sad. Soot from a pot inside one jar gave radiocarbon dates of 5 BCE to 225 CE and 70 to 370 CE. Archaeologists excavated 29 of these jars in the 1990s.

source.name: CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art: Maitum Jar No. 21

title: A Chieftain's Boat to the Afterlife
place: Việt Khê, Thủy Nguyên, Hải Phòng, Vietnam
text: Beside the Han River near Hải Phòng, Đông Sơn people buried someone in a hollowed tree trunk shaped like a boat, 4.76 metres long. Over 100 objects went with them: a bronze drum, vessels, axes and knives, a handbell, lacquered leather, spears and wooden paddles. It is the biggest Đông Sơn boat coffin found and became a national treasure in 2013.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Viet Khe boat tomb

dateLabel: Đông Sơn culture, c. 2,500–2,000 years ago
title: Four Couples on a Bronze Lid
place: Đào Thịnh, Trấn Yên, Yên Bái, Vietnam
text: This huge Đông Sơn bronze jar was made for storing food but was later used as a coffin, holding a smaller jar with ash and human teeth. Its lid shows a 12-rayed sun and four embracing couples, probably celebrating fertility. Around the body sail six boats carrying warriors with crossbows, spears and axes. It was discovered in 1961.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Dao Thinh jar

title: The Kneeling Lamp-Bearer of Lạch Trường
place: Lạch Trường, Hoằng Hóa, Thanh Hóa, Vietnam
text: A smiling bronze man kneels with an oil dish in his hands, while three S-shaped branches rise from his shoulders and back to hold more lamp dishes. His spiral hair, turban and earrings make many scholars see Indian influence. Found in a brick grave, the lamp mixes local, Chinese and Indian traditions from the late Đông Sơn period.

source.name: Vietnam National Museum of History: Bronze Lamp in the Shape of a Kneeling Man

title: Prohear's Golden Graves
place: Prohear, Prey Veng, Cambodia
text: At Prohear, one of Southeast Asia's richest Early Iron Age cemeteries, an old woman was buried with her head inside a bronze Đông Sơn drum, wearing gold bracelets, earrings and rings. A gold ring shows a man on horseback, the region's earliest evidence of horse riding. Archaeologists think the site was linked to the Yelang culture of southern China.

source.name: World Archaeology (Charles Higham): Why silence is golden

source2.name: Angkor Database: The First Golden Civilization of Cambodia (Reinecke et al.)

title: Rice Farmers on the An Sơn Mound
place: An Sơn, Đức Hòa, Long An, Vietnam
text: Just north of the Mekong Delta, Neolithic villagers built up a mound metres deep by spreading fresh layers of river soil as living floors. They grew japonica rice, a type that came from Neolithic China, and kept pigs and dogs. People buried there between about 1800 and 1200 BCE were laid out with finely made pots, some with wavy or serrated rims.

source.name: Asian Perspectives (Bellwood et al. 2011), via ANU Research Portal: An Son and the Neolithic of Southern Vietnam

source2.name: ANU Press, Terra Australis 42: Contextualising the Neolithic Occupation of Southern Vietnam

title: Non Nok Tha's First Bronze Axe
place: Non Nok Tha, Phu Wiang, Khon Kaen, Thailand
text: Non Nok Tha, dug in 1966 and 1968, was once claimed to show bronze in Thailand by 2000 BCE. Dating the skeletons themselves told a different story: the grave holding the site's earliest socketed copper-base axe dates to 980–900 BCE. Later Bronze Age burials there were given bronzes, crucibles and moulds, the tools of metalworkers.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Higham, Douka & Higham 2015): A New Chronology for the Bronze Age of Northeastern Thailand

title: A Carnelian Lion From India
place: Ban Don Ta Phet, Phanom Thuan, Kanchanaburi, Thailand
text: This Iron Age cemetery, excavated from 1975, gave what was then the earliest clear, dated evidence of contact between Southeast Asia and India. Graves held hexagonal carnelian beads, little stone lions and tigers, and thin knobbed bowls of high-tin bronze. One carnelian lion pendant was tentatively read as a symbol of the Buddha, a possible forerunner of Buddhism's arrival.

source.name: Cambridge Core (Glover & Bellina 2011): Ban Don Ta Phet and Khao Sam Kaeo: The Earliest Indian Contacts Re-assessed

source2.name: Thammasat Review (Silapanth 2018): Knobbed Ware from Archaeological Sites in Thailand

dateLabel: Iron Age, from c. 400 BCE (possibly earlier)
title: The Copper Mines of Vilabouly
place: Vilabouly, Savannakhet, Laos
text: In central Laos, ancient miners dug for malachite and smelted it in crucibles to make pure copper, which they cast on site. These mines and smelting sites date to the Iron Age, about 400 BCE to 500 CE, and possibly the Bronze Age before that. Lead isotope studies suggest Laos was a major copper supplier for Southeast Asia for about 1,500 years.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Science (Cadet et al. 2019), via James Cook University ResearchOnline

source2.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2022), via James Cook University ResearchOnline

title: The Giant-Clam Toolkit of Duyong Cave
place: Duyong Cave, Lipuun Point, Quezon, Palawan, Philippines
text: In a small Palawan cave, a muscular young man was buried face down, knees tucked under him, about 2680 BCE. Beside him lay a polished stone adze and four adzes carved from giant clam shell. He wore cone-shell ear discs, and a lime-filled ark shell by his feet probably served for betel chewing. Excavator Robert Fox called it the Philippines' first excavated Early Neolithic burial.

source.name: National Museum of the Philippines, Monograph 1 (Robert B. Fox 1970): The Tabon Caves, via University of the Philippines Diliman

title: Sumatra's Oldest Ancient Genome
place: Loyang Mendale Cave, Takengon, Central Aceh, Indonesia
text: A person buried in Loyang Mendale cave in northern Sumatra, radiocarbon-dated to 3,347 years ago, has given the earliest ancient DNA yet read from western Indonesia. They already carried a large share of Austronesian-related ancestry mixed with mainland Southeast Asian lineages. The cave's layers record Hoabinhian foragers, Austronesian arrivals and mainland influences in turn.

source.name: iScience (Xu et al. 2026), PubMed Central: Reconstructing the west-east genetic division in Indonesia using ancient genomes

dateLabel: c. 1290–1170 BCE (start of Bronze Age burials)
title: Dated by Their Shell Beads
place: Ban Lum Khao, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: At Ban Lum Khao on Thailand's Khorat Plateau, Neolithic villagers dug pits about 1400–1300 BCE, and the first Bronze Age graves followed around 1290–1170 BCE. The skeletons held no usable collagen, so scientists dated the shell beads and clam shells placed with the dead instead. The pots buried there closely match those from Ban Non Wat's second Bronze Age phase.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Higham, Douka & Higham 2015): A New Chronology for the Bronze Age of Northeastern Thailand

dateLabel: Late Neolithic/Bronze Age, c. 3,200–2,700 years ago
title: Myanmar's Ancestors Arrive From the North
place: Oakaie 1 cemetery, near Nyaung'gan, Sagaing Region, Myanmar
text: DNA read from inner-ear bones at the Oakaie 1 cemetery in central Myanmar, dated about 3,200 to 2,700 years ago, told a distinct story. Unlike ancient people at Mán Bạc, Ban Chiang and Vat Komnou, these individuals lacked an Austroasiatic genetic signature. They were closer to speakers of Sino-Tibetan languages, including people in Myanmar today, pointing to a separate East Asian origin.

source.name: Science (Lipson et al. 2018), PubMed Central: Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory

title: Newcomers in Gua Harimau Cave
place: Gua Harimau, Padang Bindu, Ogan Komering Ulu, South Sumatra, Indonesia
text: Excavations since 2012 in Gua Harimau, a cave in southern Sumatra, have uncovered 84 skeletons spanning pre-Neolithic times to the Bronze and Iron Ages. Neolithic graves, the oldest dated to about 3,100 years ago, held paddle-impressed, incised and cord-marked pottery. Skull shapes and ancient DNA reveal at least two distinct populations, backing the 'Out of Taiwan' model of Austronesian dispersal.

source.name: PLoS ONE (Matsumura et al. 2018): Cranio-morphometric and aDNA corroboration of the Austronesian dispersal model, Gua Harimau

title: The Wounded Warriors of Phum Snay
place: Phum Snay, Banteay Meanchey, Cambodia
text: Graves in this village cemetery in north-west Cambodia, used from about 350 BCE to 200 CE, held swords and other weapons. Bioarchaeologists found an exceptionally high number of injuries on the skeletons, especially to the head, most likely from fighting between people. They link these warriors to struggles between rising Iron Age chiefdoms, long before Angkor dominated the region.

source.name: Antiquity (Domett, O'Reilly & Buckley 2011): Bioarchaeological evidence for conflict in Iron Age north-west Cambodia

source2.name: Asian Perspectives (Domett & O'Reilly 2009), via ANU Research Portal: Health in Pre-Angkorian Cambodia

title: A Cemetery Found by Rubber Planters
place: Village 10.8, near Memot, Kampong Cham, Cambodia
text: Workers digging laterite for the Krek Rubber Plantation found this burial ground by chance, and archaeologists learned of it in 2001. In seven seasons from 2002 to 2008, the Memot Centre for Archaeology, with a German adviser, uncovered 56 burials with offerings, including 11 children buried in jars. The graves date between the 4th and 1st centuries BCE.

source.name: Angkor Database: The First Golden Civilization of Cambodia (Reinecke, Laychour & Sonetra)

title: Buddhism Takes Root Among the Pyu
place: Halin, Sagaing Region, Myanmar (one of the three Pyu cities)
text: From the 2nd century BCE, the walled, moated Pyu cities of Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra traded with Indic cultures, and Buddhism won its first lasting foothold in Southeast Asia, embraced by rulers and farm workers alike. The Pyu built brick stupas, kept cremated remains in urns inside shared funerary buildings, and dug water systems, some still in use.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Pyu Ancient Cities

title: New Arrivals in Bronze Age Vietnam
place: Núi Nấp, Thanh Hóa, Vietnam
text: Ancient DNA from Núi Nấp, a Bronze Age site about 2,100 to 1,900 years old, shows a big change from Vietnam's Neolithic. Earlier people at Mán Bạc were genetically close to Austroasiatic speakers, but the Núi Nấp individuals resemble present-day Vietnamese and Dai. Geneticists see substantial turnover, likely a new wave of migrants from China.

source.name: Science (Lipson et al. 2018), PubMed Central: Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory

title: Staircases of Rice in the Cordilleras
place: Batad, Banaue, Ifugao, Luzon, Philippines
text: UNESCO describes the Ifugao rice terraces of northern Luzon as built about 2,000 years ago and still farmed. Stone or mud walls hug steep mountain contours, and channels bring water from the forests on the peaks. Families pass the know-how down through generations, following a farming calendar tied to the phases of the moon.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras
